title: Objects & Classes
description: Objects, this binding, prototypes and classes

questions.explanation: Own string keys are listed in a defined order: integer-like keys first in ascending numeric order, then other string keys in insertion order. So "1" comes before "b" and "a".
?. stops and returns undefined when the value before it is null or undefined instead of throwing, and ?? then supplies the fallback. (|| would also replace other falsy values like 0 or "".)

Pulling a method off its object loses the call-site context: fn() is a plain call with no object before the dot. In a non-strict script this then defaults to the global object, which has no name property, so the result is undefined; in strict mode (modules, classes) this is undefined and this.name throws a TypeError. Keep the binding with person.getName.bind(person) or call it as person.getName().
Arrow functions don't have their own this; they use the this of the surrounding scope. Inside the regular method run, this is the team object, so the arrow callback sees team.lead.

questions.prompt: Which call rule wins when a function is called with new?
options: this is whatever object the function was bound to with bind()
this is a brand-new object created for that call
questions.explanation: new creates a fresh object, links its prototype to the function's .prototype, calls the function with this set to that object, and returns it (unless the function returns another object). new even overrides a hard bind for this.
cat has no own sound property, so the lookup follows the [[Prototype]] chain to animal. hasOwn checks only the object itself, so it is false.
Assigning dog.sound creates an own property on dog that shadows the inherited one. The prototype object animal is not modified.

questions.prompt: What does typeof report for a class?
questions.explanation: class is syntax on top of JavaScript's prototype system: a class is a special kind of function (one that must be called with new), and its methods live on Class.prototype.
Dog overrides speak, and super.speak() calls the parent class's version with the same this, so both parts are combined.

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
options: Throws a ReferenceError because this is used before super()
Throws a SyntaxError at parse time
questions.explanation: In a derived class constructor, this is not initialized until super() has been called. Touching this first throws a ReferenceError.

#count is a true private field: only code inside the class body can access it. From outside, w['#count'] is just an unrelated normal property name that doesn't exist (and w.#count would be a SyntaxError).
Static members belong to the class itself, not to instances. Counter.created is read on the class; instances would get undefined for created.
